# Tuvaṭaka Sutta (Snp 4.14 (PTS Snp 179))
**ID:** Snp 4.14 (PTS Snp 179)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Tuvaṭaka Sutta
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/snp4.14

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Tuvaṭaka Sutta* ("Speedy") is the fourteenth discourse of the *Aṭṭhakavagga* in the *Suttanipāta* (Snp 4.14, PTS Snp 179) [SuttaCentral; Salguero 2017]. The discourse sets out the attitudes, conduct, and training of a monk striving for total release [SuttaCentral], depicting the ideal bhikkhu specifically as a forest renunciant (vv. 915–934) [Ray 1994]. In verse 7, the text expounds practice (*paṭipadā*), monastic rules (*pātimokkha*), and contemplation (*samādhi*), leading modern scholars to propose that this discourse may correspond to the *Vinaya-samukase* commended in Emperor Aśoka's Bhabra Edict [Hazra 2002].
In the Theravāda commentarial tradition, the *Tuvaṭaka Sutta* is held in exceptionally high esteem. In the *Visuddhimagga* (pp. 93–94), Buddhaghosa recommends it alongside the *Rathavinīta*, *Nālaka*, and *Ariyavaṃsa* suttas as four paramount discourses that monks should consult as guides to discipline and contentment [Pagel 1992; Hazra 2002]. When classifying the canon according to the nine limbs of the teaching (*navaṅga-buddhasāsana*), Buddhaghosa singled out the *Tuvaṭaka* (along with the *Maṅgala*, *Ratana*, and *Nālaka*) as one of the specific verse texts placed under the *sutta* category [Norman 1983]. In Burma, the discourse was also incorporated into liturgical collections such as the *Catubhāṇavāra* (*Paritta*) [Kalupahana 2001].
The text's antiquity is attested by its receipt of a full canonical commentary in the *Tuvaṭakasuttaniddesa* of the *Mahāniddesa* (Mnd 14) [SuttaCentral; Norman 1983]. DharmaNexus confirms dense Pali-internal reuse with Mnd 14 (112 matches), as well as shared passages in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* and *Mahāniddesa-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. While the Pali sutta lacks a prose narrative setting, Sanskrit fragments and Chinese versions preserve introductory episodes [Norman 1983]. A curated parallel is preserved in the Chinese *Arthapada* (*Yizu jing*, T 198), where the sutta is rendered as *Dou le* (兜勒) and opens with the Buddha conjuring an illusory buddha who questions him in verse [SuttaCentral; Tournier et al. 2020]. DharmaNexus also records cross-language matches with the Sanskrit *Patna Dharmapada* and a Tibetan monastic verse treatise (*Āryamūlasarvāstivādiśrāmaṇerakārikā*, D 4127) [DharmaNexus].
